newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Killer says sorry, but S.Africa's Hani had to die.
newsitem.headline: Killer says sorry, but S.Africa's Hani had to die.

text.p: South African communist leader Chris Hani was murdered in 1993 to trigger chaos, spark a rightwing coup and end president F.W. de Klerk's "betrayal of his Afrikaner nation," one of his killers said on Tuesday.

Former rightwing politician Clive Derby-Lewis, speaking for the first time about the crime that rocked a country hardened to violence, apologised to Hani's wife Limpho as she sat at the truth commission hearing where he appealed for amnesty.
"Even today I feel remorse towards Mrs. Hani and her children, and towards the innocent people that suffered," he told the court-like session in Pretoria City Hall.
Derby-Lewis supplied the gun that Polish anti-communist immigrant Janusz Walus used to assassinate Hani, a people's hero second only to Nelson Mandela, at his home near Johannesburg.
They were sentenced to death for the killing which nearly wrecked South Africa's tortured transition from apartheid to democracy. Mandela has since suspended capital punishment.

Both men are asking the Truth and Reconciliation Commission for amnesty, which it can grant if it is satisfied they have told the full truth and that the crime was political. In their applications they admit to jointly plotting the killing, but say Walus carried it out on his own.

"I want to be seen as a fighter for the liberation of my people," Derby-Lewis said in his testimony. He is a former member of the all-white parliament for the Conservative Party that tried to stop the government's overtures to the black majority.
Hani's family is fighting the amnesty.
They will argue that the killers have not told the whole story and that Hani, the former African National Congress military chief, had espoused a peaceful settlement and was not a legitimate target.
"Chris Hani was first and foremost a soldier of his people. He was ... a military target and we treated him as such," said Derby-Lewis, a stocky 61-year-old in a dark blazer and tie.

"The fact he was also leader of the South African Communist Party and the man most likely to succeed (Mandela) as president made him also a priority political target that if successfully attacked would most likely cause our objective to be realised."
"That was to plunge the country into a state of chaos that could be used by the right to effect a takeover."

Derby-Lewis said the National Party of then president P.W. Botha and his successor de Klerk had betrayed their people by freeing Mandela from jail in 1990, unbanning the ANC and negotiating with them. The rightwing faithful had to act.
"We now had the structures for war, we were ready for war. It was in this climate that the attack on Chris Hani was launched," he said.
He said South Africa had been at war and, to some people, still was. All sides had committed sins and atrocities.
Walus, 44, will also testify at the hearing which is due to last two weeks. The committee's decision on amnesty will take longer.

Derby-Lewis, an English South African who has linked himself to the Afrikaners -- descendants of Dutch, French and German settlers -- said he believed in separate racial development in homelands, not in white supremacy.
"We weren't trying to perpetuate so-called apartheid but to secure our own place in the sun," he said, describing himself as a proud member of the white tribe of Africa.
"We are as much indigenous to southern Africa as are the Zulus."
